newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks continue bull run, but for how long?.
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks continue bull run, but for how long?.

text.p: Tokyo stocks surged past the 20,000 barrier in the Nikkei index on Tuesday for the first time since a steep slide in December, but strategists say the advance may lose steam quickly.
"Investors are biding their time, waiting to take profits somewhere between 20,000 and 21,000," said Shinichiro Takaya, senior analyst at the Yamaichi Research Institute.
"Considering the fact that there are not many concrete factors to fuel the markets higher, gains from now may be difficult to accumulate."

In little over a week, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares has risen over eight percent. It ended Tuesday's session at 20,180.92, up 666.17 points or 3.41 percent, the highest close since 20,413.46 on December 17. It was the second-largest rise this calendar year after 815 points on January 13.

Market sources said the rises so far have been inspired by pension fund allocations for the business year from April 1. The flow of new money came nearly a month earlier than last year and was a surprise for market participants, they added.

"Demand from institutional investors at the start of the new fiscal year, and massive short-covering by dealers who used margin trades to meet that heavy demand, helped the index bolt higher," a fund manager at a big life insurer said.
"But participants are limited and there are few incentives to lead the Nikkei average higher. The upside is already beginning to feel a bit heavy," he added.
Private investors have had little to do with the recent upswing, as the shares pumping up the indices were large, expensive issues beyond their reach.

Strategists said Tokyo stocks were supported by strength in the U.S. markets and a gradual realisation that the impact on the economy of a consumption tax rise may not be as horrifying as initially envisaged.

"The market environment has improved and the outlook is bullish for the time being, and in terms of valuation, Japanese stocks are at an attractive level," said Jason James, a strategist at HSBC James Capel Japan Ltd.
But the current rise stems from bundles of money which need to be spent rather than strong reasons to buy, and the rise may be temporary, he added.

"The flow of new funds into the market will last for a few months, but in the next quarter, the influence will wane and floating of Central Japan Railway Co shares could bruise fundamentals," James said.
Analysts said that despite a recent improvement in economic fundamentals, the problems of Japan's bad loan-laden financial sector has not yet been extinguished.
Such worries could flare up again in the not-to-distant future.

Yamaichi's Takaya said: "The problem-loan issue still needs to be tackled. The U.S. stock market can't continue its bull run forever and on top of that there is the question of how long Japan's ultra-low interest rates will continue."
He added: "A real recovery for the Nikkei will only come when the market has enough strength to fend off these elements."
